# CONTENTS IN THIS
## volume. Contents of these books.

### I.
### The Archidoxes <note>original: "Archidoxorum"; derived from Greek, meaning "The Greatest Doctrines" or "Supreme Wisdom."</note>.

<image-desc>A large hand-drawn brace groups the following ten numbered items, with the word "Liber" written to the left of the brace.</image-desc>

<margin>Book</margin>
1. On the mysteries of the microcosm <note>original: "microcosmi"; the "small world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>.
2. On renovation and restoration.
3. On the separation of the elements <note>original: "separatione elementorum"; the alchemical process of extracting pure substances from raw matter.</note>.
4. On the fifth essence <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the purest power or "quintessence" extracted from a physical body.</note>.
5. On the arcana <note>original: "arcanis"; the secret, eternal healing virtues found within natural substances.</note>.
6. On the magisteries <note>original: "magisterijs"; medicinal preparations that preserve the full power of their source material without separating elements.</note>.
7. On specifics <note>original: "specificis"; targeted remedies for particular ailments or organs.</note>.
8. On elixirs.
9. On external things <note>original: "externis"; treatments applied to the outside of the body.</note>.
10. On long life.

### II.

1. The Tincture of the Philosophers <note>original: "Tinctura Physicorum"; a treatise on the transformation of metals and the preparation of a universal medicine.</note>.
2. The Treasure of treasures.
3. Manual on the medicinal stone <note>original: "lapide medicinali"; the application of the Philosopher's Stone to the healing of human illness.</note>.

### III.
### Hidden philosophy <note>original: "Occulta philosophia"; the study of the invisible forces and spiritual principles within nature.</note>.

It serves as a roadmap for his revolutionary approach to extracting the "virtue" or life-force from nature for healing.</summary>

Most serene,
most powerful, most
invincible Roman Emperor,
most gracious Lord:
Since, among all the Theophrastian <note>Referring to the works of Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), the Swiss-German physician and alchemist.</note> books that have not yet come to light, the *Archidoxa* <term>Archidoxa</term> <note>Derived from Greek, meaning "The Greatest Doctrines" or "Supreme Wisdom."</note> in particular have been desired by many—so much so that even those not at all devoted to medicine have pursued them, through which Theophrastus has encountered more mockery than advancement—I have therefore wished to withhold them no longer, but to release them publicly in print.

For although I was of the same opinion as others, that such high <term>arcana</term> <note>original: "Arcana"; secret, eternal healing virtues or hidden mysteries of nature that Paracelsus believed could be extracted through alchemy.</note> should not yet be revealed to this wicked and ungrateful world...

# Preface.

...born. But one clearly sees that the opposite happens daily, from which it is to be gathered that God no longer wishes the light, which He lit in <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "medicina"</note> through **Theophrastus Paracelsus**, to remain in darkness.

Although my sole intention with this publication is to serve the common good and all well-meaning people—seeking not my own honor herein, but that of **Theophrastus**, so that he and his teachings might come to light exactly as they are—I well know that I will receive little thanks from many for it. However, because of love <note>The editor likely refers to "Christian charity" or a selfless love for his neighbor.</note>, I should rightly regard this as a small matter. For some will be angry with me that I no longer withheld these books, believing that one should not "cast pearls before swine" <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 7:6, suggesting that sacred or valuable knowledge should not be given to those who cannot appreciate or understand it.</note>. To these I answer briefly: it is true that when a thing becomes common, it quickly falls not only into contempt, and from contempt into oblivion, but also into misuse by those who do not understand it; through which much harm follows for persons of both high and low status, especially in <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "medicina"</note>.

Secondly, it is also true that among many, such great ingratitude toward God for His gifts is found as could ever be possible. But since God the Lord surpasses us with His grace, and does [not] let Himself be moved by our ingratitude, but [pours out] His blessing also in <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "Medicin"</note> somewhat more than to—

## Preface.

...reveals itself; why then should we resist the gracious will of God? For He has renewed <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "medicinam"</note>, together with the whole of Philosophy, through **Theophrastus** out of nature—just as it was in the time of the ancient patriarch **Adam** and the others—not so that it should remain hidden, but that it might become manifest to the whole world: just as **Theophrastus** indicated long ago in the *<term>Paragranum</term>* <note>One of Paracelsus’s foundational works, where he lays out the four "pillars" of medicine: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</note>, stating that his "monarchy" <note>Paracelsus used this term to describe his supreme authority or the enduring sovereignty of his system of knowledge.</note> would remain, but that of the <term>physicians</term> <note>original: "medicorum"</note> would not, and that he would judge more against the <term>physicians</term> <note>original: "medicos"</note> after his death than before it.

But what would remain of his monarchy if it were not to come to light? What would he judge after his death if his writings were to lie hidden any longer? Thus he also says in *The <term>Tincture of the Philosophers</term>* <note>original: "tinctura Physicorum," a treatise on alchemical transformation.</note> (all of which the <term>physicians</term> <note>original: "Medici"</note> should well consider and by no means cast to the wind <gloss>to ignore or dismiss</gloss>) that his theory—which proceeds from the **Light of Nature** <note>A central Paracelsian concept referring to the innate, God-given wisdom and intuitive understanding found within the natural world.</note> and, because of its constancy, can never be overturned—would begin to flourish in the year [15]58. And the practice that will follow from it will prove itself with miracles and unbelievable signs, so that even craftsmen and the common folk will understand how **Theophrastus’s** art stands against the "sloppy work of the <term>sophists</term>." <note>original: "Sophisten Sudlerei"; Paracelsus used the term "sophists" to mock university-trained doctors who relied on rhetoric and old books rather than practical experience and nature.</note>

Thirdly, there are many pious, honest people, both poor and rich, who [live] in great diffi—

## Preface.

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

...their bodily needs and are burdened with miserable diseases, to whom help and counsel may not be refused without a violation of [Christian] Charity.

In conclusion, I am moved by the saying of <term>Johann Lichtenberger</term> <note>A famous German astrologer and prophet (died c. 1503) whose "Pronosticatio" was widely influential during the Reformation.</note>, where he writes near the beginning of his prophecy thus: "He who digs out his own gold according to his pleasure, who misuses what is his own and does not trade in foreign things, does no one wrong. But he who withholds art and books does everyone wrong; he does not hide his own, but rather suppresses other people's things and steals them." Therefore, may God grant well-being and life to those who love and cultivate the Art, and thereby awaken it as if from death. All good-hearted people who have the books of ***Theophrastus*** <note>Referring to Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note> in their possession should consider this saying. They should know that although these ***Archidoxa*** <note>Paracelsus’s "Ten Books on the Archidoxes," one of his most important works on the preparation of medicines.</note>, ***Tincture of the Physicians*** <note>original: "tinctura Physicorum"; a treatise on the alchemical "tincture" or medicine of the philosophers.</note>, and the like have gone out publicly into print, they will nevertheless remain with the lovers of Art and will not become common <note>Meaning the secrets will remain hidden from the unworthy even if the text is public.</note>.

The other part [of the readers] will be full of joy and will at first thank me, in the hope that they have all the Art and secrets of Nature gathered together there and wish to become rich and blessed thereby. But when they come to the work and find nothing after much reading, effort, and expense (as will happen to many who fall upon these books <term>with unwashed hands</term> <note>original Latin: "illotis manibus"; a proverbial expression for approaching a sacred or technical subject without proper preparation, reverence, or purity of heart</note>)...

### Preface.

Then the <term>calumny</term> <note>Slander or malicious misrepresentation.</note>, scolding, reviling, and condemning will begin, and poor **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus.</note> will have to bear the brunt of it, as if he had kept the truth hidden. I ask these critics that they might consider that **Theophrastus** speaks according to the custom of the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Practitioners of a mystical tradition; here referring to the use of coded language and symbols.</note>, the natural magicians <note>original: "magorum naturalium"</note>, and all philosophers <note>original: "philosophorum"</note>. He does not always mean what the literal letter indicates, and he desires to have disciples <note>original: "discipulos"</note> for his <term>Arcana</term> <note>Secrets or hidden mysteries, specifically alchemical medicines.</note> who are practiced in those arts which he presents in the *Paragranum* <note>One of Paracelsus’s major works, defining the four pillars of medicine: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</note>. For this reason, he himself writes in the First Book of the *Archidoxes* <note>original: "Archidoxorum"</note> that in these books he wishes to speak with his own followers, and not to the common crowd <note>original: "commun"</note> of the people; rather, he wishes to write clearly enough for his own and to enclose his meaning with a good wall.

From this it follows that whoever knows nothing of the aforementioned arts will accomplish little of value in **Theophrastus’s** <term>Arcana</term>, because he does not understand what he should do or leave undone, or whether he should take "white" or "black." Much less will he provide proof if he is not experienced in the work <note>The practical, laboratory labor of alchemy.</note>. For **Theophrastus** desires—where he writes concerning the manner of administering medicines <note>original: "de modo administrandi medicamenta"</note>—that one should not administer the physical "body" <note>original: "corpus"; referring to the raw, unrefined material.</note> even in herbs, and much less is it permitted in minerals <note>original: "mineralibus"</note> and metals <note>original: "metallis"</note>. For the power, virtue, and all effect lies in the <term>Essences</term> <note>original: "Essentijs"; the internal "soul" of a substance.</note>, <term>Magisteries</term> <note>original: "Magisterijs"; refined alchemical preparations.</note>, <term>Arcana</term>, and <term>Elixirs</term> <note>original: "Elixiribus"</note>, and not in the physical body, as experience demonstrates.

<summary>The editor defends Paracelsus’s obscure writing style, arguing that medical secrets must be protected from the uninitiated and that true healing power lies in refined essences rather than raw materials.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus Paracelsus, alchemy, calumny, Cabala, Arcana, Paragranum, Archidoxes, essences, elixirs, medical theory</keywords>

### Preface.

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of those who fail to understand the work.</meta>

...[he] has not faithfully revealed the true foundation, but has hidden it with flowery words, so that no one might come to an understanding of his teaching. They claim that through this, much harm might befall the sick, and through such accusations, they would gladly make him out to be a murderer; in this, they act unchristianly. For they should consider how much good **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus.</note> accomplished and wrote, not only in **Surgery** <note>original: "Chyrurgia"</note>, concerning wounds, open sores, and the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "Frantzosen"; a common historical term for Syphilis.</note>—the likes of which no one had done before him, all of which is well understood by the industrious—but also in many **physical diseases** <note>original: "morbis Physicis"; refers to internal medicine or natural ailments.</note>. For these, he should rightly have earned more praise than ingratitude, and not be so unjustly condemned.

However, that he brought to light the **secrets** <note>original: "secreta"</note> and **mysteries of nature** <note>original: "Arcana naturæ"</note>—as they were in use among the ancient fathers, Jews, and heathens, through which they maintained long life and the body’s health—somewhat **obscurely** <note>original: "obscurè"</note>, so that not every peasant should understand them, but rather **Magically**, so that they remain with those who would be worthy of them: this cannot be held against him by any impartial person. For firstly, the **physicians** <note>original: "medici"</note> who lived in his time were themselves to blame; they blocked his printing, poisoned him with venom, and persecuted him unto death, and would by no means allow themselves to be shown the way, but remained so stubbornly set in their own tune <note>original: "auff jhrer Geigen bliben"; an idiom meaning to stubbornly stick to one's own opinion.</note>.

<summary>This page defends Paracelsus against accusations of intentional obscurity, arguing that his "Magical" writing style protected sacred medical knowledge from the unworthy and was a response to persecution by the medical establishment.</summary>

### Preface.

Furthermore, if he had described all the **secrets of nature** <note>original: "secreta naturæ"</note> in such a way that they became obvious to everyone, what would become of the **physicians** <note>original: "medici"</note>? What would be their standing among great **Potentates** <note>original: "Potentaten"; meaning powerful rulers or sovereigns.</note>, princes, and lords, if every **layman** <note>original: "idiota"; used here in the classical sense of an uneducated or common person rather than a modern insult.</note> knew how to handle the secrets of nature as well as a **physician** <note>original: "medicus"</note>? But that these things are generally unknown even to the **physicians** <note>original: "medicis"</note> of our own time is no wonder, for they conduct themselves just like their ancestors. Some despise the truth, others are too proud, others too greedy; the lazy have no desire and do not wish to **blacken their hands in the coals** <note>A reference to the soot and grime of practical alchemical or laboratory work, which many academic physicians avoided.</note>. However, those who have a desire for it and are not ashamed to learn—if they seek and persevere—will soon be delivered from darkness and human fables by Him who is the Truth and the Light.

For such high gifts are not given by God to everyone. When Christ spoke to the people in parables, and His disciples asked Him about their meaning, He said to them: "To you it is given to know the **mystery** <note>original: "geheymniß"</note> of the kingdom of God, but to those outside, everything happens through parables." Now, Christ desired to save not only the Apostles but also the poor little flock; nevertheless, He hid the **mystery** <note>original: "Geheymniß"</note> from the ungrateful **Pharisees** <note>original: "Phariseern"</note> and **Scribes** <note>original: "Schrifftgelehrten"</note>, and explained it only to His own. All Christians know...

### Preface.

Moreover, if he had described all the **secrets of nature** <term>secreta naturæ</term> <note>original: "secreta naturæ"; the hidden forces or mechanisms of the natural world.</note> in such a way that they were revealed to everyone, what would become of the **physicians** <term>medici</term>? What would their reputation be among great potentates, princes, and lords, if every **unlearned person** <term>idiota</term> <note>original: "idiota"; here meaning a layman or common person lacking formal university education.</note> knew how to handle the **secrets of nature** <note>original: "heymligkeyten der Natur"</note> just as well as a physician? That these secrets are generally not known to the physicians even in our own times is no wonder, for they behave just like their ancestors. Some despise the **truth** <note>original: "warheyt"</note>, others are too arrogant, the third group is too greedy; the lazy ones simply do not want to work and do not care to get their hands black with **coals** <note>A pointed critique of academic doctors who refused the soot-stained physical labor of laboratory alchemy or chemical medicine.</note>. But those who have a desire for it and are not ashamed to learn—if they seek and persevere—will soon be delivered from darkness and human fables by Him who is the **Truth** and the **Light**.

For such high gifts are not given by God to everyone. When Christ spoke to the people in **parables** <note>original: "gleichnissen"</note> and His disciples asked Him for their understanding, He said to them: "To you it has been given to know the **mystery** <note>original: "geheymniß"</note> of the kingdom of God, but to those outside, everything happens through parables." Now, Christ desired to save not only the apostles but also the poor little flock; nevertheless, He hid the mystery from the ungrateful Pharisees and **scribes** <term>Schrifftgelehrten</term> <note>original: "Schrifftgelehrten"; refers to the scholarly legalists of the New Testament, used here as a parallel to the university-trained doctors of the author's time.</note> and explained it only to His own. ## To the Well-Wishing Reader.

Four years ago—not for money or the sake of profit, which I certainly could have had, but for your benefit—when I published the **Archidoxa** of **Theophrastus** <note>The *Archidoxa* (The Greater Mysteries) is one of Paracelsus's most influential works, detailing his theories on the "life force" of medicines and alchemical preparations.</note> in print, it was not quite possible at that time to prevent errors <note>original: "Errata"</note> from creeping in against my will, for many reasons which are unnecessary to recount here. But because I desire to serve you, dear reader, and because all the copies I had printed were sold out <note>original: "distrahiert" – a book trade term meaning the stock was fully distributed or liquidated.</note> within two [book] fairs, I have fulfilled my promise. With my best diligence and ability, I have revised the aforementioned **Archidoxa**. I have not done this simply from other printed copies—as you will discover if you compare <note>original: "conferiern" – to compare or cross-reference.</note> mine with others—but I have corrected what was false, completed <note>original: "ergentzet" – restored or filled in missing parts.</note> what was omitted, and explained it here and there with new annotations <note>original: "Annotationibus" – explanatory notes or commentaries.</note>.

# Preface.

<note>Continued from previous page: "Ar-"</note>canum of man, as we set forth in the second book of these *Archidoxes* <note>original Latin: *Archidoxorum*. One of Paracelsus's most famous works, "The Archidoxes of Theophrastus" deals with the "highest teachings" of medicine and alchemy.</note>, and shortly thereafter mentions what we have indicated regarding the **kingfisher** <note>original German: *Eyß vogel*. In Paracelsian thought, the kingfisher was often associated with renewal, as its feathers were believed to remain fresh or even regrow after death.</note>, which he discusses in the book *On Renovation* <note>original Latin: *de renouatione*</note>. Therefore, after the first book, *On the Mysteries of the Microcosm* <note>original Latin: *de mysterijs microcosmi*</note>, I have placed the book *On Renovation* as the second, upon which the others then follow in the correct order. Nevertheless, I leave to each person their own judgment <note>original Latin: *iuditium*</note>; for I will not quarrel with anyone regarding the sequence.

->God grant that we may<-
->one day rightly put it<-
->into the work.<-

## First, Concerning Fire.

<margin>Separation of Fire <note>original: *Separatio Ignis*</note>.</margin>
Thus, regarding the element of Fire, the capturing of the four elements is to be understood as follows: When the fire burns most fiercely, capture it in a well-sealed vessel <term>receptacle; a container or flask used in chemical processing</term>. Then place it in *horse dung* <term>fimum equinum; a common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat through the natural warmth of decomposition</term> for one month. Thus you will find the four elements contained in one. Place a *receiver* <note>original: *recipiente*; a vessel used to collect the products of distillation</note> before it without using any heat; then the vapor and Air enter into it—that is *Air* <note>original: *aer*</note>.
<margin>Therefore you must let it stand until it settles into a liquid <note>original: *liquorem*</note>.</margin>
The second part is to distill *by a water bath* <term>per balneum; also known as a bain-marie, this provides gentle, even heat</term>, and so *Water* <note>original: *aqua*</note> passes over. Thereafter, distill *through ashes* <term>per cineres; a method of heating a vessel in a bed of hot ash or sand to achieve higher temperatures than water</term>, and so *Fire* <note>original: *ignis*</note> passes over, and *Earth* <note>original: *terra*</note> remains at the bottom. What the powers of these elements are, and why they are recorded here in this way, we shall report in other books.

<margin>Separation of Air <note>original: *Separatio aeris*</note>.</margin>
Likewise, Air should also be captured in a glass vessel and placed in the sun, closed with a *Hermetic seal* <term>sigillo hermetis; an airtight seal, often made by melting the glass neck of a flask to seal it completely</term>, and thus let it *digest* <term>digerieren; a process of slow, gentle heating to promote chemical change or maturation</term> throughout the *summer* <note>original: *per æstatem*</note>. In this way, the air distills and transforms into a *watery state* <note>original: *aquositet*</note>, in which it grows more and more. Separate this same quantity and let it *rot* <term>faulen; putrefaction, a process of decomposition used in alchemy to break down a substance's form</term> for one month in *horse dung* <term>fimo equino; used as a natural, steady source of warmth</term>. Thereafter, distill it *by a water bath* <term>per balneum</term> just like the Fire; more is written elsewhere regarding its powers.

### Essence, The Fourth Book.

<margin>Distinctions of the fifth essence. I.</margin>

<margin>II.</margin>

<margin>III.</margin>

<margin>Process.</margin> Dissolve the metals into a liquid and distill this downward by means of a **water bath** <term>balneum; a method of gentle heating where the vessel is placed in a container of water</term> through the act of **putrefaction** <term>putrificieren; the alchemical stage of decomposition or "rotting" used to break down a substance's structure</term>, continuing until an oil is produced from it. Afterward, distill everything over with a gentle fire; the **vapors** <note>original: *vapores*</note> will pass over first—these you should cast away. Following this, the two thick colors will pass over: one being white, and the other according to the specific nature of the metals <note>i.e., the specific color associated with that particular metal's essence</note>.

Once they have all passed over, they separate from one another in the **receiver** <term>Recipienten; the vessel placed at the end of the distillation apparatus to collect the condensed product</term>, such that the **quintessence** remains at the bottom, and the white color of the body stays on top.

Then add **distilled water twice** <note>original: *aquam distillatam binies*</note>, with which you wash it until it reaches its sweetness. Afterward, keep it; and thus the quintessence is prepared.

<margin>Reduction of the white powder. See the book of tinctures in the *Great Surgery* <note>original: *Chyrurgia magna*; likely a reference to the medical works of Paracelsus</note>.</margin>
**Reduce** the white [substance], so that it becomes a white **body** <note>original: *corpus*</note> that is malleable and metallic, and yet it cannot be identified as to what kind [of metal] it is.

<margin>False quintessences.</margin>
And although there are many more ways to extract the quintessence, we shall remain silent about them for this reason: they are not considered by us to be the quintessence, but rather **transmutations** <term>transmutationes; the alchemical changing of one metal into another</term> in which no **extractions** <term>extractiones; the process of drawing out the essential part</term> are used.

In all metals, the fifth essence is the **spirit** and the **sulfur** <term>sulphur; in alchemy, the "soul" or the oily, combustible principle of a substance</term>; therefore it is fatty. The other four elements are all **mercurial** <term>mercurialisch; relating to mercury, representing the fluid, volatile, or metallic principle</term>.

<margin>From whence the Philosopher’s Stone <note>original: *Lapis Philosophorum*</note> derives its power.</margin>
Now, for what reasons does this Stone <term>lapis; the "Stone" or medicinal arcanum</term> possess such powers that it can drive away so many strange and miraculous diseases? It does not do this through its temperament <term>complexion; the balance of the four qualities of hot, cold, moist, and dry</term>, nor through its specific form <term>forma specifica; the essential essence that defines a substance</term>, nor through its inherent property or other accidental nature. Rather, it does this through the power of the subtle practice applied to it: first through **preparations**, then through **reverberations** <term>reverberation; heating a substance in a furnace so the heat is reflected back upon it</term>, then through **sublimations** <term>sublimation; heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again to purify it</term>, then through **digestions** <term>digestion; the process of exposing a substance to gentle, consistent heat over time</term>, then through **separations**, then through **distillations**, and finally through many kinds of **reductions** <term>reduction; the act of returning a substance to a solid or previous state</term> and **resolutions** <term>resolution; the dissolving of a solid into a liquid</term>. All of these processes confirm and draw out the powers within this Stone. It is not that it possessed them from the start, but rather that they are only then bestowed upon it.

<margin>Three types of processes for stones.</margin>

### The Sixth Book.

<margin>II. Of Pearls.</margin>
**Take rectified vinegar** <note>original: "acetum correctum"; vinegar that has been distilled or purified to increase its acidity</note>, and put into it crushed and finely ground **pearls**; let them **digest** <term>Digest: To subject a substance to gentle heat over a long period to break down its components.</term> for one month. And although these appear to be simple procedures for these items, **believe one who has tried it: their operation is marvelous** <note>original: "crede experto, mirifica operatio ipsorum est"</note>. This action of their virtues is not produced by the chemist's art, but lies within their own nature, which is hidden while they are in a coarse state. In that state, it cannot work, being like a dead body; but once the **dissolution** <note>original: "resolutione"</note> is complete, its body shall be made alive. Of this, enough has been said.

I marvel especially at the virtue that God has granted to this growth, which grows so strangely and has been given such strange power.

## To Extract the Magistery from Growing Things.

<margin>Which growing things he means.</margin>

<margin>Process 1. For Wood.</margin>

## On Fragrant Specifics.

We will now speak of the **fragrant specific** <term>Specificum odoriferum: A medicinal preparation that utilizes aromatic or "spiritual" essences to drive out disease, acting on the subtle properties of the body rather than just the physical humors.</term>, in what way and form it is to be made, and especially regarding its power. 

<margin>What it is.</margin> It should be noted that a fragrant specific is a substance that drives away a patient's illness. Just as **civet** <note>original: *sibeta*; a pungent, musky substance secreted by the civet cat, highly valued in the Renaissance for its ability to mask odors and its perceived medicinal potency</note> expels **excrement** <note>original: *stercora*</note> with its scent, so too does this fragrant specific drive out the illness. 

And it is to be understood that the specific mixes into the **foul essence** <note>original: *saporrem malum*; literally "bad taste," but here referring to the offensive sensory quality or "aura" of a disease</note>, such as the stench of dung. Then, the stench of the dung can do no harm, nor does it remain; instead, it is **transformed** <term>tingiert: Related to the alchemical "tincture." It means to fundamentally change the nature or "color" of a substance by soaking it in a more powerful medicinal or spiritual force.</term>, no matter how badly it had stunk...

## I. A Remedy for Wounds.

If a medicine is to be made which, by its natural property, joins and pulls the flaps <note>or "edges"</note> of any wound together from both sides so that they stay together—just as glue fastens two boards—then this must be achieved through a powerful dryness and astringency <note>original German: *stipticitet*</note> that acts specifically upon the flesh. It is done as follows:

<margin>The Process.</margin>
Take <note>Latin: *Recipe*</note> Samech <term>Samech <note>A Paracelsian term for tartar, the crystalline sediment found in wine casks.</note></term> well-burnt and calcined <term>calcined <note>Reduced to a white powder through intense heat.</note></term> to the highest degree of whiteness. Add to it the lesser circulate <term>lesser circulate <note>Latin: *circulatum minus*; an alchemical solvent, often a distilled spirit of wine or vinegar, used to extract the "virtue" of a substance.</note></term>. Let it distill down to a dry dead head <term>dead head <note>Latin: *caput mortuum*; the solid residue left in the flask after the liquid has been evaporated or distilled away.</note></term> as thoroughly as possible, until the glass glows with heat. Afterward, pour another portion [of the solvent] in; proceed as before, and continue this until the lesser circulate remains entirely sweet, just as it is in its own nature. Following this, take it and dissolve <note>original: *resoluier*</note> it by its own means, and use what is thus dissolved.

->*Samech is tartar.* <note>original Latin: *Samech est tartarus*</note><-

->This same thing is a remedy for wounds. <note>original Latin: *remedium in vulnus*</note><-

# On Long Life

[...sicknesses] and ailments, all of which are removed through the preservation of long life and are drawn away from their very origin.

Since we wish to write about the preparation for that same long life, there are two distinctions for us to note. One is to speak **theoretically** <note>original: *theoricè*</note>. The other is to speak **practically** <note>original: *practicè*</note>. Through these two ways, the sustenance of long life is understood. And no one should wonder at this, nor should any physician be taken aback <note>original: *entferben*; literally "to lose color," meaning to be startled or lose confidence</note> by the fact that long life may be extended, for there are two causes for it. <margin>Two causes of long life.</margin> The first: no **fixed limit** <note>original: *terminus*</note> has been set for the day on which we must die; rather, we have this within our own power. The second cause is that we possess **medicine** <note>original: *Artzney*</note>, created by Him who created us, to maintain the body in its health or to drive away its sicknesses. Therefore, we are given to understand completely that death brings no sickness, nor does any sickness bring death. <note>Paracelsus often argued that death is a natural "predestination" or separation of elements, whereas disease is a treatable corruption of the body's vital forces; thus, one does not inherently necessitate the other.</note>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that human life is not bound by a predetermined date of death and can be extended through both theoretical knowledge and the practical application of medicine. # On living a long life #

<margin>Constitutions are not to be treated.</margin> <note>original Latin: *Complexiones non curari*</note>

# Of Long Life #

<margin>Our life consists of three things: 1. the **vital spirit**. 2. The **humors**. 3. The **constitutions** <note>original Latin: *Vita nostra in trib. est. 1. vitæ spiritu. 2. Humoribus. 3. Complexionibus.*</note>.</margin>
<margin>What the recipe is based upon.</margin>

Along with this, we intend to defend the **spirit of reason** <note>original: *spiritum rationis*</note> through the preservation of Nature, guarding against accidents that arise by chance from the **constitution**, such as **sadness** <note>original: *Tristitia*</note> or excessive **joy** <note>original: *Læticia*</note>, which grow and come from those things that arise from the four humors, such as **constitutions**, **qualities**, etc.

<margin>Where the medicine should be directed.</margin>

If these are without defect, then nothing evil grows from them, such as a poor constitution.

Thus the body is healthy and good.

### The Tenth Book

...stand. For example, if I held a superstition that when the ravens cry out on my roof, it were a sign that someone should die; and there are many more such examples, which it is not necessary to recount here. Such a *superstition* <note>original Latin: *superstitio*; here meaning an irrational belief or fearful omen</note> can make me sick, or even kill a person who is already ill. We attribute the cause of this to *superstitions* <note>original Latin: *superstitionibus*</note>.

<margin>Preservation and cure.</margin>
My *preservation* <note>original Latin: *conseruatio*; referring to the maintenance of health and life</note> against such *superstition* is this: I believe that this same cry is an expression of the bird's own nature, and not a sign of my own foolishness. In this way, my superstition is broken. For I cast my superstition into doubt by reflecting on my own folly. Indeed, nothing breaks a superstition except the realization that it is the work of a fool; once that is understood, the power of it vanishes entirely. For *agreement creates the deed* <note>original Latin: *consensus facit actum*; a philosophical and legal principle suggesting that an action or effect only holds power if the mind consents or believes in it</note>, and that agreement is broken by such rational understanding. In this way, I *consider* <note>original Latin: *considerier*</note> my own simplicity and the foolishness of such base belief. And this applies not only to the raven, but to all other things, which are not necessary to discuss here in this work *concerning long life* <note>original Latin: *de vita longa*; the title of Paracelsus's treatise on longevity</note>.

## To the Reader.

**T**heophrastus Bombast von Hohenheim was born of noble lineage at Einsiedeln <note>original Latin: *apud Eremitas*; refers to the Benedictine Abbey of Einsiedeln in Switzerland</note> in the territory of the Swiss <note>original: *Suenigenæ*</note>. Called "the great Paracelsus" by the Stoics <note>Paracelsus often compared himself to ancient philosophical schools, though he often challenged them</note>, he wrote two hundred and thirty books on philosophy. He also published forty-six books on the solemn practice of medicine, and edited twelve books on the Republic <note>original: *de Repub.* (De Republica); likely referring to his social and political commentaries on the common wealth</note>. He constructed seven works in the mathematical arts, and composed three works together into a single volume. Furthermore, he established sixty-six books on Necromancy <note>original: *Nigromantia*; in the Paracelsian context, this refers to the study of the "sidereal body" and the hidden spiritual forces of nature rather than "black magic" in the modern sense</note>, which are titled the *Theophrastia*. The first of these works is called *Archidoxis* <note>The "Arch-Doctrines," one of his most famous works on the chemical extraction of essences</note>, in which he explains the extractions and separations of virtues from the base matter <note>original: *ab inualido*; literally "from the infirm" or "from that which lacks strength"</note>. The second is called *Parasarchum*, in which he treats the highest good in eternity. The third is called *Carboantes* <note>This title is likely a corruption or a specific Paracelsian term related to his magical or alchemical writings; the text here breaks off mid-word</note> sa—

<margin>Slanders of the sophists <note>original: *Calumniæ sophistarū*</note></margin>

<margin>Hermes. Archelaus.</margin>

# To the Reader.

Thus, dear reader, you have the **Archidoxis** <note>original: *Archidoxa* — One of Paracelsus's foundational works on the "Arch-doctrines" or the highest mysteries of nature.</note> corrected as diligently as possible, together with the other books, as far as was feasible for me.

*The Treasure of Treasures of the Alchemists* <note>original: *Thesaurum thesaurorum alchimistarum*</note> I have placed with the *Tincture of the Physicians* <note>original: *Tinctura Physicorum*</note>, and after this the *Manual* <note>original: *Manuale*</note>, which I forgot to mention at the beginning. For these three all share one <term>scopum: a target, goal, or intended aim</term>, through which **Theophrastus** <note>The first name of Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim).</note> accomplished much good, as can still be proven today. For in Klagenfurt in Styria <note>A region in modern-day southern Austria.</note> there still lives the Warden of His Serene Highness Archduke Charles of Austria, etc., Master Anselm Best, who was a good friend of **Theophrastus**, labored much with him in the laboratory, and witnessed his <term>Curas: medical treatments or clinical healings</term>.

If he is too far away from you, however, you have an honorable man in Eberburg, three parts <note>likely referring to a distance of three leagues or miles</note> from Heidelberg: Master Georg Vetter, the pastor there, who was with **Theophrastus** in Basel and helped him record his <term>Curas</term>; he will tell you something very different than what is commonly written about him <note>Paracelsus was a controversial figure often slandered by the medical establishment of his time.</note>. I could certainly point out more people to you, were it necessary. But whoever possesses a Christian judgment will be satisfied with the books of this precious man and will not allow themselves to be overcome by envy and hatred.

->To God alone be the glory.<-

# Introduction to this book.

<margin>The Philosopher's Stone is a perfect Balsam. <note>original: *Lapis Philosophorum Balsamus perfectus est.*</note></margin>
To forge the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapidem Philosophorum*; the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and providing an elixir of life.</note> through <term>Vulcan</term> <note>original: *Vulcanum*; the Roman god of fire, used by alchemists to represent the art of fire-working and the controlled heat of the furnace.</note>, which we call the **perfect or perpetual Balsam** <note>original: *Balsamum perfectum oder perpetuum*</note> for sufficient reasons, it is first necessary for us to consider how it is materially shaped, how it becomes visible and perceptible, and also how its power or its fire comes forth and makes itself known.

<margin>Analogy of the rational fire and the Philosophical Stone. <note>original: *Similitudo ignis rationalis et lapidis Philosophici.*</note></margin>

Now, such a fire is capable of doing nothing unless it has material like itself in which it may operate, such as wood...
